hypotheses.root_cause: The main_loop task overflowed its stack and corrupted its return frame, so it faulted (BusFault escalated to HardFault) and firmware 0.9.14 crashed.
hypotheses.rationale: At 1375 ms, 135 ms before the fault, the log shows 'Stack watermark exceeded | task=main_loop used_pct=100'. That is the catalogue's tell-tale for stack overflow. The top frame of the backtrace (#00) is main_loop+0xC7, the same task. The register dump looks like a corrupted frame: LR=0xADEBF6E5 is a garbage value, SP=0xD3BBE5AE is not word-aligned, and the backtrace jumps between unrelated functions (ddr_isr, pcie_service, noc_worker, timer_cb). The other catalogue causes fit poorly. For null dereference, the null-guard pointer was 0x1024E865, which is not near null, and there is no dfar=0x0000. For a race, there is no mutex contention timeout or lock= marker. The noc_worker retry looks like a side effect, not the cause. The historical matches are hardware or thermal failure types and don't apply here.
recommended_actions: Increase the main_loop task stack (e.g. 2x) and rerun the same workload to see whether the crash goes away
Turn on stack-canary/MPU stack guard checks in a debug build so the overflow is caught at the point it happens
Get the worst-case stack depth of main_loop (call-graph analysis, -fstack-usage) and cut large local frames or recursion in the hot path
Symbolicate PC=0x0C0A21F4 and main_loop+0xC7 to confirm the faulting function epilogue/return

Null-pointer guard and service retries precede an unhandled HardFault/BusFault with a stack trace, indicating a firmware logic defect (race or bad deref) rather than a hardware fault.

- RC_FW_RACE_CONDITION: Race between service threads on a shared lock
    tell-tales: mutex contention timeout, lock=
    actions: Audit lock ordering in the contended service path; Add a watchdog-visible trace around the critical section
- RC_FW_NULL_DEREF: Null-pointer dereference in a service handler
    tell-tales: fault address near null, dfar=0x0000
    actions: Symbolicate the faulting PC and add a null guard; Fuzz the service call path with uninitialised arguments
- RC_FW_STACK_OVERFLOW: Task stack overflow corrupts the return frame
    tell-tales: stack watermark exceeded, used_pct
    actions: Increase the task stack or reduce frame size in the hot path; Enable stack-canary checks in the debug build

hypotheses.root_cause: A sustained 39 W power burst lasting 846 ms used up the thermal headroom of a die already running at 93–97 °C, and the late DVFS step-down from 1000 to 800 MHz could not stop the trip at 105 °C.
hypotheses.rationale: The only catalogue marker in the run is the workload-burst one: PMU "Power burst detected p_w=39 dur_ms=846" at 2513 ms, 33 ms after the "Temperature high t_c=95 policy=DVFS" warning. The DVFS step-down came 279 ms after the burst started (2792 ms). There are no fan markers (fan speed below profile, target_rpm) and no heatsink markers (high sensor-to-ambient delta_c), so RC_FAN_PROFILE_BAD and RC_HEATSINK_POOR have no support. VCORE stayed at 925–975 mV with droop_cnt=0, which rules out RC_REGULATOR_LIMIT. Two things lower my confidence. (1) Every sensor reads 93–97 °C right up to 3032 ms (93 °C), then the trip reports 117 °C at 3036 ms. A 24 °C rise in 4 ms is not physically plausible, so this could be a sensor or ADC glitch, or a single hot spot that the sampled sensors don't see. (2) Earlier in the same run, the firmware crashed at 1540 ms (stack watermark 100%, BusFault; this is the separate FW_EXCEPTION / RC_FW_STACK_OVERFLOW incident). That crash may have left the thermal or DVFS policy degraded and slowed throttling. Historical match: run 000015 (THERMAL_TRIP caused by RC_WORKLOAD_BURST, similarity 0.93).
recommended_actions: Re-run the same workload with the burst power capped (or the DVFS step-down triggered earlier, e.g. at 90 °C or within 50 ms of a burst) and check whether the trip goes away.

Capture the raw thermal-sensor ADC stream at high rate around the trip point, and compare the trip sensor with the others, to confirm whether the 93→117 °C jump in 4 ms is real heating or a spurious reading.
Repeat on a clean boot without the 1.5 s firmware crash (fix the main_loop stack overflow) to rule out a degraded thermal/DVFS control loop after the crash.
Log fan RPM against target and die-to-ambient delta during the burst to formally exclude the fan-profile and heatsink causes.

Prior for THERMAL_TRIP: Junction temperature exceeded the thermal trip threshold
Temperature climbed past the DVFS policy and crossed the 105C trip point before throttling could recover it, triggering an emergency shutdown — a cooling-solution or fan-profile shortfall under sustained workload.

- RC_HEATSINK_POOR: Poor heatsink/TIM contact — large die-to-ambient delta
    tell-tales: sensor-to-ambient delta high, delta_c
    actions: Re-seat the heatsink and replace the TIM; Measure mounting pressure against the thermal spec
- RC_FAN_PROFILE_BAD: Fan speed stays below the profile target as temperature rises
    tell-tales: fan speed below profile, target_rpm
    actions: Fix the fan curve / PWM mapping in the thermal policy; Verify tachometer feedback and fan power
- RC_WORKLOAD_BURST: A sustained power burst outruns the cooling headroom
    tell-tales: power burst detected, p_w=
    actions: Cap the burst power or lengthen the DVFS step-down reaction; Add thermal headroom to the test's power envelope
